newsitem.title: KENYA: Both sides lose with Kenya general strike call.
newsitem.headline: Both sides lose with Kenya general strike call.

text.p: A test of strength between the authorities and opposition groups gave Kenya a day of marches, clashes, some looting and an incomplete general strike. Neither side appeared to have gained from the uproar.

For the alliance of opposition groups demanding reform from President Daniel arap Moi, 73, the day was at best a mixed success with only relatively small rallies and many workers defying their call for a one-day national strike.
The police, for the first time since the reform campaign took to the streets in May, suffered more dead than the protesters.
Police said a total of three people, two of them policemen, were killed in Nairobi and in and near the town of Kiambu, 10 km (six miles) to the north, and one policeman was seriously wounded.

The toll contrasted with nine dead, none of them policeman, on July 7 when riot police brutally broke up reform rallies in Kenya, bringing international condemnation down on Kenya and forcing the authorities quietly to rein in their forces.

Opposition and pro-reform alliance leaders who addressed a rally in Nairobi's Uhuru park declared Friday's strike a great success but many shopowners -- especially from the Asian community -- only closed out of fear of violence and looting.
Barely 1,000 activists attended the rally in Uhuru park which began on an ugly note when gangs of youths chased down and beat several suspected police spies.
One of those beaten was Gilbert Ahanya Simiyi, who was held down barely conscious as youths said he was armed with a gun and knife and was an inspector in the police special branch.
Simiyi was pronounced dead on arrival at a Nairobi hospital while opposition leaders told the crowd of the sweeping constitutional reforms they demand of Moi, ruler for 19 years.
In a statement, police later said he was an off-duty policeman who was passing and was badly injured in a "fracas" with pro-reform protesters who, they said, had injured many other people.
The police "noted with satisfaction" that many people ignored the strike call but said two other people were killed.
The statement said police were attacked by a large mob on a main road out of Nairobi barricaded by pro-reform demonstrators and fired 32 teargas rounds and one round of live ammunition.
The bullet hit a man, an "attacker", the police statement said, in the leg and he died in treatment at Kiambu hospital.
Police said the third person to die on Friday was a police inspector killed as he was driving home to Kiambu when his car overturned as he was stoned by a large mob barricading a road.

In Nairobi, hundreds of youths at the rally's end ran into the largely deserted city centre, breaking shop windows and chanting "Moi Must Go". They stoned vehicles and blocked roads until paramilitary police fired in the air to disperse them.
Moi, seeking a new five-year term at general elections this year, has succeeded in dividing some opposition leaders by promising some political reforms and calling for dialogue.
Police said a total of six shops were damaged and one looted, 14 civilian and six government vehicles were damaged and a total of 24 people were arrested in Kenya on Friday.
In Nairobi's vast Mathare slum unemployed youths set up barricades of burning tyres and clashed with riot police. They also attacked a bar which stayed open and looted iron sheets.
As well as Kiambu, witnesses reported clashes and looting in the towns of Nyahururu, Karatina, Kerugoya, Thika, Nyeri and Githunguri in the opposition heartland of Central Province.
Two opposition parliamentarians were arrested in the western town of Kisumu for allegedly inciting people to strike.
But Kenya's shilling, which sank to a record official low against the dollar on Thursday after the IMF halted a key loan package citing official corruption, regained 1.76 percent by Friday's close.
